lesson.subtitle: Lesson 38 — How Do You Really Feel?
lesson.title_tag: Professor View — Vanessa Giuriati | Lesson 38 — How Do You Really Feel?
lesson.grammar_point: -ed vs -ing adjectives for feelings and their causes (frustrated / frustrating) + make someone feel

listenings.text: Here is a mistake that can be a little embarrassing. A student once told her teacher, I'm so boring today. Her teacher smiled and said, no, you're not boring at all. You're bored! What's the difference? Words that end in e-d describe how a person feels: bored, tired, interested, confused. Words that end in i-n-g describe the thing that causes the feeling: a boring meeting, a tiring trip, an interesting book. So if a movie is confusing, you feel confused. If your job is exhausting, you feel exhausted. Here is a simple test. Ask yourself: is this the feeling, or the cause? The feeling ends in e-d. The cause ends in i-n-g. And if you say, I'm interesting, well, that may also be true. But it's a very different sentence.

Hey Vanessa, it's Paulo. I just wanted to tell you about the marathon on Sunday. Honestly, the first ten kilometers were exhausting, and at kilometer thirty I was so frustrated with my legs that I almost stopped. But then I saw my kids holding a sign with my name on it, and I felt so motivated. When I crossed the finish line, I was over the moon, and so relieved it was over. Now I'm a bit fed up with walking, though. My legs hurt every time I take the stairs. Anyway, call me back. I want to hear about your week.

extra_audio.text: First, I stop and notice how I feel. Then I choose a precise word: not bad, but frustrated. After that, I say what caused it: the meeting was frustrating. Next, I say what I will do about it. In the end, I ask the other person: how about you?

paras: When someone asks "How are you?", most of us say "fine" or "busy". But many coaches say that naming a feeling more precisely makes it easier to manage. "Bad" is a big, confusing word. "Frustrated" or "let down" is a small, clear one.

Think about a difficult week. If you only say "I'm stressed", the problem feels huge. If you say "I'm overwhelmed by my inbox, and I'm a bit on edge about Friday's presentation", you already know where to start: the inbox first, then the presentation.

It works with good feelings, too. "Happy" is nice, but "relieved" tells you that a worry has gone, and "thrilled" tells you that something exciting has happened. Precise words also make conversations more interesting, and people feel closer to you.

So this week, try a simple exercise. Every evening, write down one feeling from your day and one thing that caused it. After a few days, you will see patterns, and it is surprising how calm that can make you feel. -- Laura, wellbeing coach
